claims.text: Coupling high-throughput free-energy simulations with calibrated high-temperature DSC and dilatometry provides an integrated method for characterizing melting in high-entropy alloys.
The integrated method can determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties within approximately ±10% error.
The approximately ±10% performance applies across a wide range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The target initial state is a crystalline HEA solid before melting.
Thermodynamic integration and metadynamics can calculate the free-energy differences underlying solid-to-liquid phase transitions in HEAs.
The simulated free-energy profile and calorimetric and dilatometric responses capture the relevant solid-to-liquid phase-change phenomena.
Calibrated high-temperature calorimetry can translate the transition response into precise latent heat and entropy-of-fusion measurements.
Calibrated dilatometry can accurately determine the volume change associated with melting.
Combining simulations with experimental calibration ensures accurate capture of latent heat, entropy changes, and volume changes.
The integrated results will agree within approximately ±10% with traditional CALPHAD assessments, stand-alone high-temperature calorimetry, and independent atomistic simulations.
CALPHAD is an established baseline for assessing phase equilibria and thermodynamic properties.
Combining theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic information can produce descriptions that agree with measured thermodynamic properties.
The integrated method will significantly reduce experimental and computational resource requirements relative to the baseline methods.
Extreme atomic-size mismatch can make the approach less reliable because interatomic potentials may fail.
Unexpected contaminant phases can make the approach less reliable because experimental calibrations may fail.
The proposed measurements include liquid-phase specific heat and viscosity.
The approach is falsified if more than 40% of tested alloy compositions deviate from benchmark values by more than ±10%.
